text1: The Rasho-pattern escort corvette is a light support vessel, built to shepherd larger Covenant warships rather than duel alone. Its integral suppressor beam weakens the shields of anything that threatens its charges, generous energy shielding lets it screen a flank or cover a withdrawal, and a short-range slipspace drive lets it flicker across the battle to wherever it is needed. Lightly armed for its class, it relies on the fleet it escorts; isolated and swarmed, it has little answer.

The Ceudar-pattern heavy corvette is the Covenant's frontline gunboat, a compact hull that trades range for a heavy forward punch. A hardpoint-mounted plasma cannon and two flanking pulse lasers let it press an engagement hard behind its energy shield, and a high energy focus system overcharges its guns for a short, brutal burst that can break a target's guard. Deadly in a straight fight, it is undone the moment nimbler ships get onto its flanks.

The Ardo'nikapoora-pattern landing corvette is a troop and materiel transport, its hull given over to holds and boarding craft rather than weapons. A single point-defense emitter and a strong energy shield are its only protection, and a slipspace drive lets it slip away from a losing fight. It is not built to trade fire; caught without an escort, it survives only by running.

The SDV-class heavy corvette is the Covenant's dedicated screen, a destroyer-weight hull bristling with point-defense emitters and layered energy shielding. It exists to smother incoming missiles and strike craft around a battle group, freeing the line ships to fire unhindered, and a point-defense overdrive lets its turrets briefly track anything that moves. Its own guns are defensive by design; left to fight alone it can hold, but it cannot press, and a determined swarm will eventually saturate its arcs.

The CPV-class escort carrier trades the destroyer's guns for a pair of launch bays, projecting Covenant strike craft from behind a heavy shield. Slow and thinly armed, it hangs at the rear of an engagement and lets its wings do the fighting, using a short slipspace drive to reposition or disengage. Cornered without its screen, it is little more than a slow, valuable target.

The CRS-class strike destroyer is a fast, aggressive hull built to close and overwhelm. A forward plasma cannon backed by a plasma torpedo battery lets it dump a devastating alpha into a single target before its shield buckles, and a plasma burn lets it pick its fights and abandon the ones it cannot win. Fragile for its weight, it lives or dies on the opening exchange; drawn into a grind against numbers, it loses.

The Ket-pattern assault destroyer is a long-range energy platform, its broad hull built around a single heavy spinal plasma lance. Vast flux reserves and a high-energy focus let it land punishing aimed shots from beyond most return fire, and its energy shield lets it stand its ground while it works. Slow to turn and reliant on that one great gun, it is dangerous at range and vulnerable to anything fast enough to get inside its arc.

The CCS-class battlecruiser is the backbone of a Covenant battle group and its usual command hull. A heavy spinal projector flanked by turreted emitters lets it dictate an engagement from the front, and its powerful energy shield lets it hold the line while lighter ships maneuver. Versatile and well-rounded rather than specialized, it is formidable head-on but can be pulled apart if allowed to be flanked and swarmed.

The DDS-class escort carrier is a fast fleet carrier, fielding three wings of Covenant strike craft from behind a strong shield. It carries only enough weaponry to fend off attackers while its fighters do the real work, and a targeting-feed array relays firing solutions to its wings to sharpen their attacks. Kept at range behind an escort it is a potent force multiplier; run down and boarded, it has little to offer in a straight fight.

The ORS-class light cruiser is a fast, hard-hitting hull built to strike and reposition. A forward plasma lance and paired autocannons deliver a brutal frontal salvo, and a plasma burn lets it dash into or out of range at will. Lightly built for a cruiser, it depends on speed and its shield to survive; caught flat-footed by numbers, it burns down quickly.

The RCS-class armored cruiser is a bulwark, trading firepower for sheer endurance. Heavily armored and wrapped in a deep energy shield, with a damper field to blunt incoming fire, it is built to anchor a battle line and refuse to break. Its guns are fewer and more measured than its tonnage suggests, so it grinds down opponents slowly rather than deleting them; its danger is that it simply will not die.

The ORS-class heavy cruiser is a Covenant capital ship in all but name, a battle-line dreadnought fielding a spinal projector and a broadside of heavy emitters. A displacement drive lets a hull this size reposition with alarming speed, and its shield is deep enough to trade blows with anything short of a supercapital. Rare and jealously guarded, a single ORS can be the deciding weight in a fleet action.

The CPV-class heavy destroyer is a fast, wide-hulled assault cruiser built to run down and shatter smaller warships. A forward energy projector, paired autocannons and flanking emitters deliver a heavy frontal weight of fire, and a plasma burn gives it a closing speed no ship its size should have. It carries less armor than the battle-line hulls, betting instead on speed, shield, and shock; kept at range by disciplined fire, it loses the edge that makes it dangerous.

A battleship known only from fragmentary records, the Reverence-class is the immovable heart of a Covenant battle line. Enormous armor and the deepest energy shielding of any battle-line hull let it soak punishment that would gut a lesser ship, and a fortress shield system hardens that shield further when the fire is heaviest. Its energy projector, plasma lance and heavy batteries grind the enemy down while it holds. It is slow and ponderous, and asks its escorts to keep the swarms off it; given that, it simply does not fall.

The CAS-class assault carrier is a Covenant flagship, a vessel a full tier above the battle line and built to break fleets by itself. Its forward hemisphere bristles with heavy guns: an energy projector, twin plasma lances, autocannons, a bombardment battery and plasma torpedoes. Behind them sits a shield deep enough to weather two dreadnoughts at once, and the ship carries its own strike wings to finish what the guns start. Its slipspace drive can tear open a rupture wide enough to carry the whole fight around it, friend and foe alike, to another part of the battlefield. All that power points forward: its speed is glacial and its flanks and stern are thinly covered, so fast ships that reach the blind spot behind it can work unpunished where nothing swings to bear.

The CVS-class supercarrier is a mobile fortress-hangar, fielding nine wings of Covenant craft from behind a heavy shield. It mounts almost nothing for direct assault, only a pair of heavy plasma torpedo batteries for long-range support, a few beams and a dense skin of point-defense, and instead wages war entirely through its swarms of fighters and bombers. Immensely valuable and nearly defenseless up close, it must be screened at all costs; stripped of its escort, it is a slow, enormous prize.

The Seraph is the Covenant's frontline space-superiority craft, a heavy, well-armored fighter that fills two roles from the same airframe: a gun configuration that duels and escorts, and a bomber configuration that carries plasma torpedoes against capital hulls. Sturdier than the strike craft it faces, it survives runs that would gut a lighter bomber, and its Sangheili pilots press attacks with a discipline that unnerves human squadrons.

The Type-26 Banshee is a light, fast attack craft thrown into battle in great numbers. Individually fragile and lightly armed, it relies on speed and sheer count, swarming enemy strike craft and harrying the flanks of larger ships until their point defense is overwhelmed. Cheap to field and quick to replace, a cloud of Type-26s is less a squadron than a weather front.

The Type-27 Banshee is the heavier cousin of the Type-26, rebuilt as a dedicated interceptor. Faster and better armed than the swarm craft it flies alongside, it runs down enemy fighters and bombers before they reach the battle line, its long attack runs and elite handling making it the Covenant's answer to hostile air. Rarer and costlier than its little sibling, it is flown by the fleet's best.
Opens a slipspace portal ahead of the ship and translates it up to 500 units toward the targeted point. The drive stores up to three charges, regained one at a time.

The far aperture of a slipspace rupture. Pass through it to emerge in normal space.

A hotter, wider cousin of the plasma beam emitter, the suppressor beam is the integral weapon of the Rasho-pattern escort corvette. Its continuous stream of plasma does modest damage on its own, but every moment it plays across a shield destabilises the field and leaves it more vulnerable to everything else that hits it. Escort crews use it to soften targets for the heavier ships they protect; by itself it wears an opponent down rather than breaking it.

The energy projector is the weapon the Covenant reserves for its greatest hulls: the same heavy lance its fleets once used to scour whole worlds to glass. After a long charge it fires a sustained beam that does ordinary damage against shields and armor, but where it finds bare hull it burns deeper with every second and punches clean through, striking whatever lies behind the target. The mount cannot traverse while it fires and needs a long cooldown, so a projector ship must line up its shot; a target that keeps moving or keeps its defenses up blunts the worst of it.

Despite its name, the pulse laser turret fires a rapid stream of plasma bolts rather than a beam. Found by the dozen on every Covenant hull, it is the fleet's standard point-defense mount, filling the space around a warship with fire fast enough to shred missiles and strike craft. Its reach is short and its bolts lose their bite against armored warships, so it protects far more than it kills.

The plasma repeater is the standard armament of Covenant strike craft, a compact cannon that throws heavy, ionising bolts. Each hit carries a strong electromagnetic charge, and bolts that reach armor or hull can arc into a target's weapons and engines, leaving it crippled for the craft that follow. Its raw damage is slight; it is the massed fire of a whole wing that makes it dangerous.

The lightest of the Covenant plasma torpedoes is sized for strike craft: a fast, self-guided bolt of contained plasma carried by Seraph bombers. Against armor or hull the plasma clings and keeps burning after the hit, eating away the armor around the strike. It burns out over a short flight and a launcher carries only two rounds, which return slowly, so bombers must close in before they release.

The plasma beam emitter is the Covenant's general-purpose support beam, a steady violet stream usually fitted in pairs. It does little damage by itself, but a beam held on a shield destabilises the field and makes every other hit on it count for more, and several emitters on one target compound the effect. Ships that rely on it need heavier guns alongside to turn that pressure into kills.

The plasma cannon is a heavy ship-mounted gun that hurls large, self-contained balls of plasma, the workhorse of the Covenant's medium mounts. Each round hits hard enough to trouble shields and armor alike, and its steady rate of fire keeps an opponent under constant pressure. Its cost is heat: a ship that leans on its cannons builds flux quickly and must pick its moment to break off.

Adapted from the siege mortars of Covenant ground armor, the plasma mortar launches slow, heavy blobs of plasma that burst on impact and splash the area around the hit. It is built to break armor and punish targets that bunch together, and does comparatively poor work against shields. Its rounds fly straight and slowly and fade harmlessly at the end of their range, so it rewards gunners who lead a slow target.

The plasma torpedo is the Covenant's standard anti-ship ordnance, launched in salvos of four from medium batteries. Each torpedo is a self-guided bolt of contained plasma that tracks its target over long distances and, on striking armor or hull, keeps burning, melting the armor around the impact. Magazines are deep but slow to refill, so a battery is best saved for a target whose defenses are already failing.

The plasma lance trades the energy projector's sustained burn for a single searing pulse. After a brief charge it lashes out with a short burst of superheated plasma that tears into armor, then needs several seconds to recover. It is a precise, punishing weapon against armored warships and a poor one against shields, which shrug off much of its heat.

The plasma autocannon is a heavy rapid-fire mount, a warship-scale descendant of the Seraph's cannons. It empties its magazine in a long, hammering stream of bolts that overwhelms point defense and strike craft and keeps shields under pressure, then has to wait while the magazine slowly recharges. Fired in short bursts it can be sustained; held down, it leaves its ship briefly toothless.

The plasma bombardment cannon is a siege battery, the ship-mounted cousin of the anti-air emplacements the Covenant plants on contested worlds. It gathers a visible charge before each shot, then hurls a massive plasma bolt that detonates in a wide burst, battering armor across the area and shoving smaller ships aside. The charge gives targets warning and the bolt is slow, so it is deadliest against large, slow or distracted hulls.

The heavy plasma torpedo is the Covenant's capital-killer, a single enormous bolt of contained plasma launched from the largest batteries. It is slow and ponderous in the turn, but a hit will gut nearly anything, its clinging plasma melting a wide swath of armor around the impact. Point defense and fast ships can stop or evade it, and the battery reloads slowly, so it is fired at committed targets that cannot dodge.

Projects a full-coverage energy shield from emitter rings woven into the hull. Raising it takes several seconds as the field sweeps along the ship. The shield absorbs hits from its own energy reserve instead of raising flux, and regenerates once it has gone a short while without being struck. If the reserve is exhausted, the shield collapses and must reset before it can be raised again.
text3: A full-coverage shield that absorbs hits from its own regenerating reserve and collapses when depleted.
text5: Each hit is blocked completely and drains the reserve by {{30%}} of its damage, whatever the damage type; the hit that empties the reserve carries its remainder through. The field takes {{6}} seconds to raise. Regeneration pauses after each hit, runs at {{50%}} for the following {{3}} seconds, slows once flux passes {{50%}} and stops at maximum flux. Capacity, regeneration and recovery times depend on the hull.

text1: Overclocks the ship's targeting computers and turret drives for a few seconds. Weapons track far faster, automated fire aims with machine precision, and energy weapons reach further, letting a screening ship swat down a sudden wave of missiles or strike craft.

text5: For {{6}} seconds, weapon and beam turn rate are increased by {{300%}}, autofire accuracy is maximized and energy weapon range is increased by {{25%}}.

text1: Tears open a slipspace rupture off the bow wide enough to swallow a battle. After a long charge, everything close to the portal is pulled through with the carrier: allied and enemy ships, strike craft, even missiles in flight. All of it emerges together at the chosen point. The translation is violent: any ship caught without its shields up is damaged, and the effort leaves the carrier's flux banks nearly full.
text3: Carries the ship and everything around it to a distant point on the battlefield.
text5: Charges for {{8}} seconds and requires flux below {{70%}}. Takes everything within {{1000}} su of the portal to a point at least {{2000}} su away. Ships without their shields up lose {{10%}} of their maximum hull. The carrier is left at {{80%}} flux or more. Cooldown: {{60}} seconds.

text1: Analyst's note: Covenant power and fire-control systems are built around their energy weapons. Plasma mounts draw on dedicated containment fields that extend their reach and ease their heat load. The same systems resist human maintenance; without the Huragok who normally tend them, crews struggle to keep a Covenant hull at full readiness.

Analyst's note: Covenant hulls are clad in nanolaminate, a composite that appears to be grown rather than forged. It shrugs off heat and blast well enough to survive a plasma exchange, but kinetic test rounds crack it more easily than Domain plating, and its low mass is a large part of why these ships move as quickly as they do.

Analyst's note: the field is projected along the whole hull rather than spread from a single emitter, and it runs on its own reserve instead of the ship's flux grid. Yard crews who have fitted one to a Sector hull report that it works, that feeding it draws heavily on the ship's flux capacity, and that nobody can quite explain why.

Analyst's note: the Huragok are the Covenant's engineers: buoyant, many-limbed beings that may be animals or machines and seem to exist only to repair and improve technology. Covenant systems are designed on the assumption that Huragok are aboard; with them, a ship holds its readiness and mends its own hull mid-battle. How any came to serve aboard Sector fleets is not understood. They do not appear to mind.

Analyst's note: a Covenant slipspace drive can be tuned far beyond its factory settings by anyone patient enough to learn its logic. A tuned drive recharges faster between combat translations, and a fleet of tuned drives holds its slipspace corridor open for a quicker transit.

Analyst's note: an auxiliary capacitor bank that feeds plasma mounts faster than their designers intended. Recovered Covenant manuals treat it as an emergency measure. Human crews tend to leave it on.

Analyst's note: Covenant vent cycles can be routed through the weapon containment fields, dumping the stored charge into the next volleys instead of into space. Recovered gunnery manuals describe it as a way to break a stalemate; the longer the ship has been holding heat, the harder the opening blow.

Analyst's note: a fire-control lattice that learns a target's shield and armor harmonics the longer it stays engaged. Sangheili gunnery doctrine prizes it. It rewards the patience to stay on one target, and punishes a captain who chases everything that moves.

Analyst's note: weapon emitters run past their rated thresholds, firing faster as the ship's flux climbs. Recovered maintenance logs call it a practice of desperate crews, and document at length the overload cascades that follow a mistake.
Analyst's note: a denser emitter lattice that spreads the shock of each hit across more of the field, so every impact draws less from the reserve.
Analyst's note: additional reserve cells give the shield a deeper pool to draw on. A larger reserve is slower to stabilise, and waits longer after each hit before it begins to refill.
Analyst's note: re-sequenced emitter rings bring the field up far faster and restart its regeneration sooner after a strike. Covenant skirmish craft appear to carry them as standard.
Analyst's note: isolates the shield's reserve from the ship's flux grid, so the field keeps recovering while the ship runs hot.
Analyst's note: a thinner, faster-cycling field favoured by raiders. It holds less in reserve, but recovers between passes.
